figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Comparison of distillation strategies. (a) DMD uses a bidirectional teacher’s prediction as the reference for the current chunk. (b) AR distillation directly uses the history-conditioned prediction of an AR teacher as the full target. (c) History Forcing uses the context residual between the AR teacher’s predictions with and without history to correct the reference prediction.
figures.headline: Schematic shows History Forcing corrects the DMD reference with a history residual, while AR distillation uses the full history-conditioned target.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Fig. 2, DMD with a bidirectional diffusion teacher provides strong supervision for video quality, but does not explicitly incorporate distant autoregressive history into teacher predictions.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Overview of History Forcing. An AR teacher predicts the same noisy student chunk with and without additional history. The resulting history contrast modifies the reference score in DMD and the velocity target in on-policy self-distillation.
figures.headline: Overview: an AR teacher predicts a noisy student chunk with and without extra history, and the contrast modifies both DMD and velocity targets.
citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 3, this correction is applied to the reference score in DMD for long-horizon consistency and to the teacher velocity target in on-policy self-distillation for out-of-sight evolution.
As illustrated in Fig. 3, we construct $h^{i}$ for each supervised student chunk using latent frames from the teacher’s fixed-camera rollout at timestamps preceding the start of that chunk.

figures.caption: Comparison of distillation targets, where $+$ and $-$ denote distributions with and without additional history. (a) DMD uses a reference close to the data distribution without history. (b) AR Distillation uses the history-conditioned AR distribution, with larger modeling error. (c) History Forcing transfers the history-induced shift from the AR teacher to the reference, producing a target closer to the data distribution with history.

abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient generation, yet maintaining consistency over long rollouts remains challenging, especially when subjects or scenes reappear after going out of sight. Despite progress in fidelity and rollout robustness, existing distillation methods do not fully exploit richer historical information to constrain the student’s current prediction. To address this gap, we introduce History Forcing, a unified on-policy distillation framework that strengthens historical supervision for few-step autoregressive video generators. The framework uses the residual between teacher predictions with and without informative historical context to decouple this supervision. Such a historical context can be obtained using earlier generated chunks with less accumulated drift or a fixed-view teacher rollout that keeps the scene visible while the student looks away. The residual is then weighted and added to the score or velocity prediction used for distillation, forming a corrected target. By aligning the student with this corrected target through distillation, History Forcing incorporates long-range historical constraints into autoregressive generation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance among 1.3B models, with a VBench quality score of 85.07 for 15s video generation and a VBench-Long aggregate score of 79.82 for 60s generation. For out-of-sight world modeling, evaluations further demonstrate more plausible scene evolution and more consistent states when the camera returns, with Evolution Quality improving from 2.35 to 2.70 on PlayWorld and Object Consistency from 58.43 to 62.18 on MemoBench.

sections.body: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion models drift over long rollouts, and information about subjects or scenes that leave the view may be insufficiently used when they reappear. The paper argues that existing distillation targets do not explicitly strengthen historical constraints. Matching the full distribution of a history-conditioned autoregressive teacher ties history supervision to that teacher's visual quality, which the authors call history–quality coupling. History Forcing instead computes a residual between teacher predictions with and without history and adds it to the distillation target. For long videos, the history comes from earlier generated chunks. For out-of-sight world modeling, it comes from a fixed-camera teacher rollout. The reported VBench scores are 85.07 for 15s generation and 79.82 for 60s generation.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: History Forcing adds a history-based correction to distillation so long video rollouts keep subjects and scenes consistent.

sections.body: The related work covers three groups. Training-free and autoregressive methods extend long-horizon video diffusion through cache compression, rolling denoising, and history-aware supervision. Few-step causal distillation methods, including CausVid, Self Forcing, and Context Forcing, use distribution matching or teacher-student alignment. Video world models add memory mechanisms, such as geometry-indexed view retrieval and scene memory, to support revisits. The authors state that these methods improve consistency, but that the contribution of historical context remains implicit in the distillation target and that coherent continuation across long observation gaps remains challenging.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work adds history through memory or training changes, but leaves the contribution of history implicit in distillation targets.

sections.body: This section defines the notation used by the method. A clean latent is noised with a linear interpolation, and the network predicts a velocity, from which a clean estimate and a score are derived. Autoregressive video diffusion factorizes the video into chunks, each generated conditioned on previous chunks. Distribution matching distillation trains a few-step generator by matching a reference distribution given by a pretrained diffusion model. Its gradient uses a reference score and a fake score, where the fake score is estimated by an online denoiser trained on student-generated samples. Both scores are computed from denoising predictions.
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: Background defines flow-matching velocity, chunk-wise autoregressive factorization, and distribution matching distillation gradients.

sections.body: For the current chunk, the method runs an autoregressive teacher on the same noisy sample with and without additional history. The score difference between the two predictions is added to the reference score: $s_{\mathrm{HF}}=s_{\mathrm{ref}}+\lambda\left(s_{\mathrm{AR}}^{+}-s_{\mathrm{AR}}^{-}\right)$, where $\lambda$ controls the strength of historical supervision. For long videos, the extra history is the chunks preceding a shared recent context, and the corrected score replaces the reference score in the distribution matching update. For out-of-sight revisits, a fixed-camera teacher rollout supplies history, and the corrected velocity target is trained with a mean squared error loss on revisit chunks. The authors state that this objective decouples history supervision from matching the full autoregressive distribution.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: History Forcing adds a history-contrast residual to the reference score for long videos and to velocity targets for revisits.

sections.body: The 15s evaluation uses VBench, and the 60s evaluation uses VBench-Long on MovieGenBench prompts. Students are initialized from Causal Forcing checkpoints, and the bidirectional teacher is Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B. The 15s comparison evaluates released checkpoints of competing models. On 15s generation, the method reports a quality score of 85.07. On 60s generation, it reports an aggregate score of 79.82, exceeding Rolling Forcing by 0.60 points. On out-of-sight revisits, Evolution Quality rises from 2.35 to 2.70 on PlayWorld, and Object Consistency rises from 58.43 to 62.18 on MemoBench Real. The PlayWorld subset has 43 cases and the MemoBench Real subset has 164 clips.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: History Forcing scores highest among 1.3B students on VBench-Long and improves out-of-sight revisit metrics on both benchmarks.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the method as decoupled history supervision that augments DMD with long-range constraints while keeping the bidirectional teacher's visual supervision. For world modeling, fixed-view teacher history guides out-of-sight evolution through the velocity target. The authors state that the main limit is the underlying models' ability to capture temporal dynamics. Limited scene evolution in fixed-view teacher rollouts can weaken supervision for out-of-sight state changes. Experiments are limited to 1.3B models for long videos and a 5B backbone for world modeling. Future work will explore larger teachers and students, longer-context training, and better simulation of physically plausible dynamics.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: History Forcing reduces drift in long videos and keeps object states across out-of-sight gaps, within limits set by the base models.

sections.body: Appendix A gives training, inference, and evaluation settings. Both applications use AdamW, 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, and 4 SDE steps with unshifted timesteps (1000,750,500,250). Outputs are generated at 16 FPS. For long-video training, the student learning rate is $2\times 10^{-6}$, and the 10s AR teacher uses the fine-tuning checkpoint at iteration 2500. For world-model training, LoRA rank is 64 and the learning rate is $1\times 10^{-5}$. Appendix B shows additional qualitative examples, including sand filling, coffee pouring, 15s chapel and carnival scenes, and 60s toothbrushing, dumpling, guitar, and kitchen examples.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists training, inference and evaluation settings and additional qualitative examples for both applications.
